column2: When the chair bearers asked where to go, Hu hesitated. He ought to call on Third Granny Yu, but it would be inconvenient after dark. If he returned to Jinchang Inn, there would be no reason to come into the city again, and wasting the whole evening at the inn seemed a pity. Caught between the two, he thought of a third destination: Pan Shuya's house. Yet a call after dark might seem discourteous. Besides, Pan would ask about the business he had entrusted to him, and Hu needed to consider his answer carefully. Better not meet him in haste. Then he thought of a fourth possibility. “Tell me, do you know where a famous courtesan called Huang Yinbao lives?” The bearer smiled apologetically. “I'm afraid not.” “Where are most of the houses in Suzhou?” “Along Shantang. Dingjia Lane in Shangtang has the most. We could carry you there and ask.” Hu had no time to search from house to house for a beauty. Even if he found her, it would mean no more than drinking with Qiu Fengyan in her company; nothing useful would be done. He made up his mind: back to the inn first.

As soon as he reached Jinchang Inn, he saw Zhou Yiming, who greeted him as though he had found a treasure. “Mr Hu! I've been waiting all afternoon.” Before Hu could answer, a young man stepped forward. Tall, fair and extremely presentable, he had a delicate, almost feminine face. Hu felt he had seen him somewhere before and stood speechless for a moment. “This is Fushan,” Zhou explained. “A’qiao's brother.” “No wonder! I thought you looked familiar, as though we'd met before. That explains it. You and your sister look very much alike.” Somewhat shyly, Fushan said, “Master Hu.” His Suzhou accent sounded even more feminine. Then he knelt and kowtowed. “Get up, please!” His sister had specifically insisted on this courtesy. Hu had to pull and lift him to his feet. He was very pleased, though he could not tell whether it was the young man's fine appearance or affection extending from the sister to the brother that pleased him. “I went to Mudu early this morning,” Zhou said, “especially to bring him to meet you.”

“No wonder you didn't come this morning.” Hu turned to Fushan. “How old are you?” “Nineteen.” “You've been learning the cloth trade?” “Yes.” “For how many years? Have you finished your apprenticeship?” “I finished a year ago.” In only a few questions, three discrepancies had emerged. Hu's memory was excellent, and he remembered what A’qiao had told him. “Isn't your childhood name A’shun?” “Yes. When I entered the cloth shop, the proprietor called me Fushan, and the name stuck.” “I remember your sister saying you were eighteen and hadn't finished your apprenticeship.” “I'm nineteen. My sister remembered wrong.” “But surely she couldn't be mistaken about whether you'd finished?” Zhou explained for him. “You could say he has, or that he hasn't. His training is complete, but by custom he must serve his master for another three years. That term isn't finished yet.” “Is everything settled now?” Hu asked Zhou. “All settled. We've got his apprenticeship contract back.” “Good.” He turned to Fushan again. “Your sister has entrusted you to me. Tell me, what would you like to do?” “I should like Master Hu to...” “Don't call me Master,” Hu interrupted. “Call me Mr Hu.” “Yes, sir!” Fushan too had found “Master” awkward on his tongue and gladly adopted the new form of address.

“Since you've learned the cloth business, I suppose you can judge silks and satins?” “I can, but the shop was small and didn't stock much. There are some costly silks I've never seen.” “That doesn't matter. I'll take you to Shanghai, where you'll have the chance. The most important tool in business is an abacus.” “He's good with one,” Zhou put in. “Very quick.” “Then let me test you. Get an abacus and sit down.” Once Fushan was ready, Hu casually gave him a problem. Four bolts of cloth cost ten taels in all. Their lengths differed: forty-seven, fifty-six, thirty-two and forty-nine chi. What was the price per chi? He spoke quickly. Besides testing the boy's abacus, he wanted to test his intelligence. If he could remember all those troublesome figures after hearing them once, he had promise. Fushan did not disappoint him. His fingers flew, and the beads clicked briskly and smoothly. The sound alone, like “large and small pearls falling onto a jade dish”, showed an expert hand. When it stopped, he reported, “The four bolts total a hundred and eighty-four chi. At ten taels altogether, each chi costs five li, four hao, three si and four hu of a tael, with a fraction left over.” Hu checked it on the abacus himself and found it correct. Thoroughly satisfied, he nodded. “You can learn this business. But a good memory and quick reckoning will only take you as far as small business if your other abilities fall short. Large business needs another set of skills, more than I can explain at once. Stay with me, and you'll understand in time. Today I'll tell you one thing: to get on in the world, you must keep your word. Before promising anything, consider whether you can do it. Don't promise what you can't do; once you've promised, you must do it.” Fushan nodded earnestly throughout, then answered respectfully, “I'll remember.”

“Do you know Suzhou well?” “Not the city itself.” “What about Shantang?” “I know Shantang. Which part do you want, sir?” “I'm not going myself. I want you to run an errand. There's a courtesan called Huang Yinbao. Two friends of mine are there, one named Qiu and one Liu. Find out what they're doing and come back to tell me.” Hu added at once, “Don't let them know anyone is making inquiries.” “Yes, sir.” Fushan answered calmly and rose. He seemed to hesitate briefly, but soon left. When he was out of sight, Zhou spoke with mild disapproval. “I know you're testing his ability to handle himself, Mr Hu. But such places hardly suit a young fellow like him.” “Afraid he'll fall into a web of enchantment?” Hu laughed. “Never fear. From the look of him, he's already spent some time in one. I'm not so much testing him as seeing how well he knows his way around. Better enter the garden of pleasure young than in old age. I employ people differently from others. They want young men with old heads. I want young men with ability and experience, who've seen and been through everything. Then, when it matters, they won't be dazzled and deceived.” This was a view Zhou had never heard before. He had no answer at first, though reflection suggested there was some sense in it. Still, young men who had all seen the world and learned its tricks might be hard to control. At last he understood. “Only you could keep them in hand, Mr Hu. Other people wouldn't dare do things your way.” “Exactly!” Hu was pleased. “Now you understand me.” Zhou still worried about Fushan. “But he hasn't much money. Even if he finds the Huang house, how will he get through the door?” “That depends on his resourcefulness. Never mind him for now. How is A’qiao?”

“Still at the Pans'. She's grown plumper, so she must be living comfortably. Fushan's business was settled only two or three days before you arrived. If you hadn't come, I'd already have taken him back to Shanghai. What are your instructions now?” Hu sighed and shook his head. “One thing after another—it's like holding a handful of tangled hair. I can't answer you yet. You and Fushan had better stay here for now.” Zhou went upstairs to arrange rooms. Left alone, Hu leaned against his pillow, resting without sleeping and considering his affairs one by one. He realized that he had made a grave mistake and thought of the saying, “A gentleman attends to the essentials.” His own essentials were banking first and silk second. For the bank, Pan Shuya's money was ready to hand. New silk would soon reach the Huzhou market. Was he going to trade in it this year, and if so, how? He must decide promptly and tell Chen Shilong what to do. If he kept attending to incidental matters and neglected his proper business, he would end in an impossible position. He therefore made a firm decision. Tomorrow he would hear what Yang Fengmao had to say. If the business proved troublesome, he would follow Qiu's suggestion and leave the guns in Shanghai for the time being, then hurry back to Zhejiang with the Seventh Lady and attend to real work. He would deal with other matters if he could; if not, they must wait. Having settled that, he made further arrangements, assigning manageable tasks to others. Liu could look after the Pan family's business; Zhou could handle He Guiqing and A’qiao. The mere change of outlook lifted much of the weight that had burdened him for days. Neither man would do his task as well as Hu himself, of course, and it was hard not to worry. But he was exhausted and could no longer attend to everything. Resolving to let go, he recalled two lines of verse seen somewhere and recited them aloud: “Shut the door and push the moon beyond the window; leave the plum blossoms to decide things for themselves.”

Of the three incidental matters, however, one could not be neglected. With his thoughts concentrated, he could consider it more thoroughly. Why travel all the way back to Hangzhou and then turn towards Huzhou? There was a canal from Suzhou to Huzhou. Suzhou lay east of Lake Tai and Huzhou south of it; that ought to be the shorter route. “Old Zhou, how does the water route from Suzhou to Huzhou run?” “Do you mean the canal? I've travelled it. From Suzhou to Wujiang it's called the Beitang River; from Wujiang to Pingwang, the Guantang River. At Pingwang it divides. The southern branch to Jiaxing is the Nantang River. The western branch, through Nanxun to Huzhou, is the Xitang River. A hundred and twenty li altogether.” Hu made up his mind. He trimmed the candle, ground ink and wrote a letter himself. Just as he finished sealing it, Fushan returned.

“Huang Yinbao lives at Shuitantou in Xiatang,” Fushan reported. “Mr Liu and Mr Qiu are both there. Mr Liu is banking at pai gow.” “Pai gow?” Hu was surprised. “With whom?” “The people of the house—older maids and young maids, a whole roomful. Only Mr Qiu is drinking.” Hu laughed. “One a drunkard, the other a gambler. They're the same wherever they go.” “Did you see them yourself?” Zhou asked. “How did you know who they were?” Fushan blushed. “I know an attendant there. He's from Mudu too. I asked him to take me in and show me.” This lent some support to Hu's suggestion that the youth had already ventured into the web of enchantment. Zhou smiled and said nothing, while Hu praised him. “Very capable. You can find your own way when you're out on an errand. Good! Have you ever been to Huzhou?” “No.” Encouraged by the praise, Fushan volunteered at once. “But that doesn't matter. If you need something done, I'll go.” “Take a letter for me. The address is on the envelope. Call the man Uncle Four. Get his reply and come straight back.” Hu handed him the letter and ten taels, adding, “One may live frugally at home, but must have money on the road. Take enough; account for whatever you spend.” This meant that actual travelling expenses would be reimbursed. Zhou thought of explaining, but then reflected that Hu might deliberately be testing Fushan. Better not reveal the point. He kept silent.

Fushan inquired that night about the passenger boats to Huzhou and left early the next morning. Hu rose late, refreshed himself and waited for news from Yang Fengmao. Meanwhile, he gave detailed instructions for arranging A’qiao's marriage to He. Liu and Qiu returned from spending the night at Huang Yinbao's, bringing the inevitable round of jokes. Soon it was time for the noon gun. Yang kept his word and hurried back while they were gathered round the lunch table. All four rose and invited him to join them. He had already eaten, so Hu did not press him, but took him into the inner suite for another private talk. “When did you get back?” “This morning. I had a few things to say at Third Granny Yu's.” Yang paused, blinking repeatedly, as though he had much to say and did not know where to begin. This put Hu on his guard. Yang had gone to the Yu house instead of coming straight to the inn. Clearly, “their own people” had held a private discussion unsuitable for outsiders. It seemed they had not yet reached the point of sharing fortunes and misfortunes. Hu must judge carefully how close they really were. “Uncle Hu, first there's something I must mention. Third Granny Yu hopes to claim a connection above her station by taking your concubine as her sworn daughter. Would you consent to honour us in that way?” This was wholly unexpected. But Hu's mind worked quickly; several thoughts flashed through it, and he grasped the probable intention. They had only just met, and the business they were discussing involved great differences between safety and danger, good fortune and disaster. Only a family tie making them “their own people” would reassure them. For the public business, he would gladly agree; the closer personal connection would be welcome too. But he had another concern. If Furong acquired such a powerful sworn mother, she might become impossible to control, creating future trouble between wife and concubine. He hesitated to consent.

Men of the brotherhood knew how to change course with the wind. Seeing his hesitation, Yang said hastily, “Of course, it was presumptuous to seek such a connection. If it can't be managed...” “No!” Hu interrupted, afraid of being misunderstood. Only the truth could remove suspicion. “Third Granny Yu honours us more than I could wish. The difficulty is that my wife is a tigress. I don't even dare take my concubine home. If my wife behaves violently and my concubine suffers, I shall have wronged Third Granny Yu. That's why I dare not agree.” The words were candid yet tactful. Yang understood their deeper meaning. “On that point, set your mind at rest. Third Granny Yu knows the ways of the world through and through. She'll only help settle your household troubles.” He waved his hand emphatically. “She'll never back her sworn daughter against you and make things difficult.” “Then what more can I say?” Hu assumed an expression of complete satisfaction. “Rather than choose a day, let us take the day we have. My concubine shall kowtow to Third Granny Yu this afternoon.” “Good. Leave the arrangements to me. To be frank, Uncle Hu, this will give my master something to say to the other side. Everything had been agreed; it was hard to go back on his word. Now he can say, ‘This concerns my sworn younger sister's family. There is truly no alternative. I can only apologize.’” Only now did Hu understand why Yang had first gone to the Yu house. The arrangement involved Third Granny Yu and had to be explained to her beforehand. It had taken considerable thought and showed the Yu family's sincerity. He was reassured.

“And the other matter?” Hu asked. This was the great question of accepting an amnesty. Yang answered steadily. “My master naturally favours it, but it won't be easy. It's like a boat already running east with the current. Turning back to travel upstream against the wind is hard work. He would like you to come and discuss it face to face.” “Certainly.” Hu agreed without hesitation. “Where is he now?” “In Tongli. You know the place?” Naturally, Hu had heard of it. Wujiang's county town was tiny; people joked that a shout of “Hello” at the east gate would be answered at the west. Tongli, northeast of the county town, was a famous large market town within the county. Bordering Qingpu, it was one of the richest parts of the southeastern land of fish and rice. “So he's in Tongli. No wonder you could go and return within a day. When shall we leave?” “Early tomorrow. Would that suit you?” “Yes. How do we go?” “By boat, of course. I'll arrange it. Riding is convenient too; one embankment road takes you straight there.” “Better go by boat.”

“Very well.” Yang paused. “But there's something I should tell you first. Several of the other side's leaders are in Tongli too. Would you like to meet them?” Hu considered, then answered firmly. “Without entering the tiger's den, how can one get its cub? I'll meet them.” “Then you'll have to go along with their ways. They're reckless womanizers and gamblers, a worthless lot. But if you'll mix with them, anything can be discussed.” An idea struck Hu. “Brother Yang, may I bring someone?” “Naturally.” Yang sounded a little reluctant. “Who would it be?” “Someone entirely trustworthy and one of our own: Third Master Liu, just outside. We're related. Food, clothes, women, gambling—he knows them all, and gambling is his particular expertise.” “If he's your relation, naturally there's no difficulty.” Yang rose. “I'll report to Third Granny Yu.” “Good. I'll follow shortly. Tell my concubine first that I'm very pleased she'll become Third Granny Yu's sworn daughter. I'll provide whatever the ceremony requires.” “No.” Yang interrupted. “Third Granny Yu was quite explicit. She's already ashamed to have accepted your generous gifts and won't let you spend more.” Hu thought there was no need to argue now. He could simply follow the proper forms himself. He gave a vague, accommodating answer. As soon as Yang had gone, he summoned Qiu, Liu and Zhou to discuss how to divide the work.

The business was complicated, and the amnesty involved matters that could not be spoken of freely. He could not explain everything at once and gave only the essential instructions. First, Zhou was to go into the city and buy lengths of cloth and other gifts for Furong to present to her sworn mother. Second, Liu must pack and prepare to leave for Tongli the following day. Finally, Qiu was to go to the Yu house and discuss the adoption ceremony with the Seventh Lady. “What about you?” Qiu asked. “Why not come to the Yus' with us?” “There's somewhere important I must go first. I'll join you there shortly.” The important place was Pan Shuya's house. Yang's words had inspired Hu to try an unconventional approach: he would use gambling as an opportunity to win over those rough adventurers. For that he needed ample capital. He had only a little over ten thousand taels in banknotes with him and meant to borrow twenty thousand in silver from Pan.

As soon as his visiting card went in, Pan came out to welcome him. “Xueyan, you deserve a penalty! Why didn't you come to see me when you reached Suzhou?” “How did you know I was here?” “I saw Education Commissioner He this morning. He told me.” “I see. Naturally, I deserve a penalty. But consider: why would I call on him unless something made it unavoidable? I hadn't even meant to disturb you. I know wealthy gentlemen like yourselves dislike pointless social calls. Since I couldn't spare time to amuse you, and haven't finished the business you entrusted to me, what was the use of coming?” Pan laughed. “I can never outtalk you. Does that mean you've come on business today?” “Yes. One doesn't visit the temple without a purpose. I have two favours to ask. First, I'd like you and your friends to support me in Tongli.” “What long arms you have!” Pan interrupted. “Reaching all the way to Tongli to make money.” “Exactly the opposite. I'm going to give some away, not make it. Otherwise I wouldn't have had to trouble you. I mean to gamble on a grand scale.” Now Pan understood what “support” meant. Hu was no gambler, though, and why should he travel so far for a great gambling session? “There must be a reason?” “Certainly. There are people I want to befriend. You'll understand when we reach Tongli.” Hu followed immediately with his second request. “For that purpose, I'd like to borrow twenty thousand taels. When my money arrives from Shanghai in three days, I'll repay you at once.”

“Why talk of ‘at once’ or anything of the sort?” Pan thought for a moment. “Would gold leaf do?” “Certainly. If I borrow gold leaf, I'll repay you in gold leaf.” Pan lent him five hundred taels of gold leaf. But he was less interested in supporting him in Tongli. “The place is mad for gambling. Even ordinary families will entertain for three days when a son turns one or a grandson reaches his first month, and gamble for all three days. All sorts mix together there. I don't want to go.” “Then I won't press you. If this business goes well, I'll have a proper game with you all when I come back. There's someone I want to introduce too: a very amusing fellow who'll get on well with all of you. I've put your business in his hands as well. We'll discuss everything when I return.” “Good. We shall await you.” Pan then asked, “Would you like to see our other guest?” He meant A’qiao. Hu had already decided what to do and answered at once, “No need. I know she's staying with you and has grown plumper. A contented mind makes a well-fed body. She's comfortable, and I'm quite at ease.” He took his leave, returned first to Jinchang Inn and locked the gold leaf in his chest. Zhou then arrived with an ample assortment of ceremonial gifts. Hu inspected them one by one and was satisfied. With Zhou accompanying the gifts behind his chair, they went into the city together.

At the Yu house, Yu Shaowu opened the main gate to receive him. Looking inside, Hu saw a pair of tall red candles burning in the hall, along with incense shaped like the character for longevity. The tables and chairs had fresh red satin covers embroidered in gold. Four new palace lanterns hung beneath the eaves. Everything was festive, arranged like a birthday celebration. Furong had not yet performed the ceremony, but Shaowu had already changed his form of address. “Uncle! Everything is ready. We've only been waiting for you to begin.” Within, distinguished guests filled both sides of the hall. Qiu had been given a place of honour, with several men keeping him company. When Hu appeared, their attention naturally shifted. Third Granny Yu clearly regarded the adoption as a great event. As he exchanged courtesies, he wondered whether she simply felt an affinity with Furong or had some other intention. There was no immediate answer, so he went along with the occasion. Finding an opening, he told Shaowu, “I'll go in and pay my respects to your grandmother first.” “She's waiting for you, Uncle. I'll take you in.” Excusing himself to the company, Hu followed through the inner gate. The rooms within were festive too. The Seventh Lady came forward smiling, wearing a green jacket and black skirt, with a large, deep-red camellia at her temple. Against her snow-white skin, the colours looked especially vivid. She curtsied. “Congratulations, Little Uncle!” “You honour me.” Hu returned the greeting with clasped hands. “Thank you for all your help these past two days.” “Little Uncle, come here a moment.” She was too impatient to wait for Third Granny Yu. Hu realized that she must have something he should know before meeting the old lady. He sent an apologetic glance across the room and followed her aside.

“We must treat it as though Auntie Furong became Third Granny Yu's sworn daughter as a child,” she said softly. A man of the world needed only a hint. This would make it easier for Yu Wucheng to explain his position. Otherwise, the adoption would plainly look like a deliberately staged performance. “I understand,” Hu said at once. “Third Granny Yu has brought out the private savings from the bottom of her chest to entertain everyone today. It will be a grand evening.” “Ah, that reminds me. I meant to ask: everything seems very elaborate. Is it because she likes Furong, or has she another purpose?” “Both. She wants to give Auntie a celebration, and she wants word to spread through the brotherhood that she's adopted a sworn daughter.” “Ah! Old ginger is the hottest indeed.” They entered the main inner room together. Third Granny Yu and Furong wore matching clothes: bright-red lined jackets of Ning silk and pale-blue skirts, all brand-new, seemingly made overnight. To honour Third Granny Yu and raise Furong's standing, Hu addressed her directly as “Mother”. The old lady was pleased, and Furong more pleased still. Having the famous Third Granny Yu of the Yu family as her sworn mother was a great comfort. What troubled her was that, as a concubine, she could not wear a red skirt even on such a day. Third Granny Yu wished to show her consideration without breaking customary rules. After consulting the Seventh Lady, she had engaged four seamstresses, set up worktables and had these two matching outfits made overnight, so that anyone could see they were mother and daughter. Furong was deeply grateful already. Now Hu's use of the same address effaced the distinction of her lesser status and delighted her further. “Master Hu,” Third Granny Yu said, her smiling eyes narrowing to slits, “I shall presume on this connection and call you ‘son-in-law’ from now on.” Holding Furong's hand tightly, she continued, “Now we're truly one family. You must keep Wucheng's affairs in mind.” “Naturally. I must attend not only to Elder Brother's affairs, but to Shaowu's too.” These were more than ordinary courtesies. Hu understood that this was a performance for their friends in the brotherhood. Taking Third Granny Yu's cues, he answered every word perfectly, leaving no opening. All the formalities were solemn and dignified. The ceremony passed smoothly, followed by a banquet of twelve tables. With Qiu as his “escort”, Hu went round offering toasts, attending to everyone with great care.

The banquet was followed by gambling: the dice-shaking game, pai gow and everything else. Hu did not join in this time. Accompanied by Yang, he passed through the inner gate to take leave of Third Granny Yu. “Mother, I'm going to Tongli to see Elder Brother tomorrow. Have you any message for him?” “Nothing for him. But I have a few words for you, son-in-law.” “Please tell me.” “I'm very happy today. To be honest, I'm more than halfway into the grave. To have such an unexpected joy now—Heaven has treated me well.” “Well said, Mother.” Hu smiled. “I'm only afraid Furong and I haven't done enough for you. Once Elder Brother and I have settled this business, I'll take you to Hangzhou to spend the summer by West Lake.” “Good! I went there to offer incense last year and mean to go again this year. But that is for later. Leave it for now.” She paused. “Son-in-law, I have something very important to entrust to you.” Hu felt slightly uneasy. “Why put it that way? I've already said I'll do everything I can. Elder Brother's affairs and Shaowu's are my own.” “I know. But although your elder brother is no longer young, some of the things he says and does are very immature. He's far less seasoned than Fengmao, and farther still from you.” Hu smiled. “Mother, you make him sound so bad that even I feel inclined to defend him.” “He's my own son, and my only one. Why would I deliberately belittle him? It's simply the truth. Before outsiders, I must cover his shortcomings. Before you, I needn't. You'll see in time. What I ask is really a warning: if Wucheng says or does anything improper, please bear with him for my sake.”

Hu found this puzzling, but there was no time to examine it closely. He readily agreed. “Set your mind at rest. When I meet him, I'll respect him as my own elder brother. He's always had a great tree to shelter under, and I've heard that he's had a young master's temper from childhood. Whatever he may say, I certainly won't take offence.” “Son-in-law!” Third Granny Yu was moved. “Those words are a blessing to the Yu family. I need say no more. When you return, I'll give you a proper welcome.” “A welcome and a celebration of success,” Hu added to please her. “May your golden words come true.” She turned and called, “My lady, come out.” She meant Furong. With Yang present, Furong had not felt free to appear earlier. At the summons, she came out with measured, dignified steps. “These past two days have counted as a visit to your mother's home. Your husband has come to fetch you today. Go back together.”

If Furong went back now, she would have to return tomorrow when Hu left for Tongli. Why make the needless journey? Staying where she was would also demonstrate her devotion to her new mother. Furong paid close attention to such social considerations. Having decided, she smiled. “I'm more comfortable here with you, Mother. I'm not going back.” Hu did not want her to go back either. That night he had matters to discuss with Liu and Qiu. They might talk late, or go to Huang Yinbao's to drink through the night. With Furong present, he would have to watch both his words and his movements. Her answer suited him perfectly, and he supported it at once. “Let her stay and keep you company. I'll fetch her when I return from Tongli.” “As you please. This is your home too. Or you could stay here yourself.” “There's no need. Brother Fengmao and I still have a little business to discuss.” Hu seized the chance to take his leave. “We set off early tomorrow, so I'll say goodbye now.” He bowed. After exchanging reminders and good wishes, he and Qiu found Liu at a gambling table. Yang accompanied them back to Jinchang Inn, where they agreed when to board the boat next day. He then left.

“I don't think Yu Wucheng will be easy to deal with.” Hu looked troubled. “I must have another force in reserve.” He asked Zhou, “Do you know Tongli?” “I know all the waterways and landing places in this district.” “Good.” Hu turned to Qiu. “Once we've left tomorrow, you and Old Zhou follow us. Find an inn, stay there and wait for my message. You'll have to put up with it for a day or two. Neither of you must leave.” “Very well.” Qiu smiled. “I've bought two collections of poetry and haven't opened them yet. I can drink and read at the inn.” “Exactly. That will do.” Hu asked Zhou, “Which inn? Decide now.” Zhou thought for a moment. “I can't recall any inn in Tongli. Whenever I've passed through, I've stayed on the boat or at a friend's house. I've never used an inn.” “Then we'll send messages through your friend's house,” Liu suggested. “Good. He's in your line of business, Third Master Liu. Go to East Street in Tongli and ask for the proprietor of Yanghetang Pharmacy. You'll find me.” Hu nodded. “Settled. Once you've found lodgings, Old Qiu must stay out of sight. Old Zhou can inquire along the waterfront about what Yu Wucheng is doing in Tongli. But keep it discreet.” “I understand.”
